watchForNext.neutral: Short words may start to come out whole instead of sound by sound, and letter pairs like 'sh', 'ch' and 'st' stop being a stumbling block. You might also hear their reading voice begin to follow the story, not just the letters.

variants.charlotte_mason: Listen for words from reading lessons recognised at a glance somewhere else, on a shop sign or in a favourite poem, and for new words worked out with growing confidence.
variants.classical: As phonics practice settles, listen for 'sh', 'ch' and 'th' read without a pause, and for reading aloud that flows from word to word rather than stopping on each one.
variants.montessori: After building words with the moveable alphabet, watch for the child reading back word cards on their own, and for interest in the phonogram work: 'sh', 'ch', 'ai'.
variants.waldorf_steiner: Reading often grows out of writing here. Watch for the child reading back the verses and sentences in their main lesson book, then spotting those same words in other places.
variants.unschooling: Look for words read out in the wild, from cereal boxes, game cards or street signs, and for the moment they would rather read something themselves than wait to be told.
variants.eclectic: Whatever reading program you use, the clearest sign is often outside it: a word read at a glance on a menu or game card, and letter pairs like 'sh' handled without a pause.

watchForNext.neutral: Small sums may start arriving without fingers or counting, and you might hear a shortcut explained out loud, such as 'seven and three make ten, so seven and five is twelve'. Some children also begin checking a take-away by adding it back.

variants.charlotte_mason: In short mental arithmetic lessons, listen for facts recalled at once, and for a quicker way being found and explained in the child's own words.
variants.classical: As addition and subtraction facts are recited and drilled, watch for them pulled from memory mid-problem, and for skip-counting chants turning into early times tables.
variants.montessori: After work with the bead bars and strip boards, watch for the child setting the materials aside for facts they already know, and returning to them by choice to check.
variants.waldorf_steiner: Listen for number facts surfacing in rhythmic games and clapping verses, and for story problems solved in the head before the counting stones come out.
variants.unschooling: Watch for quick mental maths in real situations: working out change, splitting lollies evenly, or tallying points in a board game without counting each one.
variants.eclectic: Whether it shows up on a workbook page or in a board game, look for facts that come from memory, and for a favourite trick like doubles or making ten used on purpose.

watchForNext.neutral: You might start to hear comparisons between books, like 'this is like the other dragon story', and questions about why the author chose something. Some children also begin to notice when they've lost the thread and flick back a page to find it.

variants.charlotte_mason: Watch for narrations that link this book to another living book, or that add the child's own opinion of what a character did.
variants.classical: In the questions that follow a reading, listen for answers that point back to the text, 'because it says...', and for comparisons between two stories on the same theme.
variants.montessori: Watch for the child seeking out a second book on a subject they enjoyed, and for their own questions about why a character or author did something, raised without a prompt.
variants.waldorf_steiner: When the story is retold the next day, listen for the child's own pictures entering it: what a character felt, or how this tale echoes a fable told before.
variants.unschooling: Look for comparisons popping up unprompted, between two books, a book and its film, or a story and something that happened to them, along with 'why did they do that?'
variants.eclectic: Across read-alouds and their own reading, listen for 'this is like...' comparisons, and for questions about why the author made a choice as well as what happened.

watchForNext.neutral: Writing may begin to keep pace with their thoughts, so a sentence gets finished before the idea slips away. You might also see the first joins between letters, or hear a request to learn 'running writing'.

variants.charlotte_mason: In copywork, watch for a full line written beautifully with less effort, and for the care given to a favourite passage carrying over into their own labels and notes.
variants.classical: As copywork and dictation become routine, watch for a dictated sentence written at speaking pace, and for even, tidy letters holding up across a whole page, not just the first line.
variants.montessori: Watch for the control built through the metal insets showing in steady, even letters, and for writing chosen as work in its own right: labels, lists, notes to family.
variants.waldorf_steiner: Form drawing often prepares the hand for joined writing. Watch for the flowing, connected forms in their main lesson book beginning to appear between letters too.
variants.unschooling: Look for writing that has a real job, a sign for the bedroom door, a birthday card, a list for the next game, and for it getting quicker and easier for others to read.
variants.eclectic: Whatever handwriting program you follow, watch for the neatness of practice pages carrying over into cards, labels and their own stories, where nobody asked them to be neat.

watchForNext.neutral: Numbers may start to be pulled apart in more than one way, like hearing 38 as 30 and 8, or as 20 and 18. You might also notice them checking whether an answer looks about right before they say it.

variants.charlotte_mason: With bundles of sticks and real coins in short lessons, listen for numbers split in more than one way, and for the child noticing when an answer can't be right.
variants.classical: As counting by twos, fives and tens becomes memory work, watch for those chants used as tools: counting a pile of coins in tens, or jumping along a number line in fives.
variants.montessori: After work with the golden beads, watch for the child building larger numbers from beads or number cards without help, and making the exchange of ten units for a ten bar on their own.
variants.waldorf_steiner: Number work here often starts from the whole. Listen for delight in finding all the ways twelve can be split, and for skip counting carried by clapping and stepping games.
variants.unschooling: Look for bigger numbers turning up in play: counting a jar of coins in tens, reading house numbers, or guessing how many pages are left in a book.
variants.eclectic: Whether it's place-value blocks or the coins in a money box, watch for numbers split up in different ways, and for a quick 'that can't be right' when an answer is off.

watchForNext.neutral: You might see them wanting to record what they notice, with a quick drawing, a photo or a few words, and coming back later to compare. Listen too for 'I saw...' being kept apart from 'I think...'.

variants.charlotte_mason: Watch for the nature notebook becoming the child's own: a brush drawing of a leaf with the date and place, made without being asked, and a return visit to see what has changed.
variants.classical: Look for observations written up in an orderly way, a labelled drawing, the date and a sentence of what was seen, and for the same specimen checked again to compare.
variants.montessori: Watch for specimens on the science shelf sorted, matched and compared with care, the magnifier picked up unprompted, and observations recorded with a drawing or label.
variants.waldorf_steiner: Watch for observations carried into a drawing or painting in the main lesson book, and for the child noticing how the same tree or creek looks different as the season turns.
variants.unschooling: Look for their own ways of keeping track: a photo series of the tadpoles, a drawing of the bird that keeps visiting, or a collection they keep adding to and sorting.
variants.eclectic: Watch for noticing turning into recording, whether on a science workbook page or as a photo on the tablet, and for 'I saw' being kept separate from 'I think'.

watchForNext.neutral: Pictures may start to carry a feeling or a story, not just a subject, with colours and sizes chosen on purpose. You might also notice a style that's recognisably theirs, or hear them explain why they drew something the way they did.

variants.charlotte_mason: After picture study, watch for something from a studied artist turning up in their own work, and listen for a painting described from memory in rich detail.
variants.classical: As they learn the words for line, colour and shape, listen for that vocabulary used to explain their own choices, and watch for a master's work copied with growing care.
variants.montessori: With materials freely available on the art shelf, watch for longer projects the child chooses and returns to over several days, and for colour and medium chosen for a reason.
variants.waldorf_steiner: In wet-on-wet painting and block crayon drawing, watch for colours chosen to carry a mood, and for main lesson book pictures that tell the story as much as the words do.
variants.unschooling: Look for art made for their own purposes, a comic, a poster for a backyard show, a portrait given as a gift, with choices they can tell you the reasons for.
variants.eclectic: Whether it comes from an art lesson or free time at the table, watch for colour and size chosen on purpose, and for a style you'd recognise as theirs.

watchForNext.neutral: You might notice a plan appearing before the build, either a quick drawing or a clear 'I'm going to make...'. Watch too for testing what they've made and changing it when it doesn't work, like a bridge that keeps falling over.

variants.charlotte_mason: In handicrafts and free building, watch for a plan described beforehand, and for a wobbly part rebuilt until it holds rather than abandoned.
variants.classical: Watch for a build described in order before it starts, first this, then that, and for the child explaining afterwards what worked and what they would change.
variants.montessori: Watch for longer building projects chosen and returned to, with the child spotting their own mistakes and fixing them as the build itself shows what went wrong.
variants.waldorf_steiner: Building with blocks, branches and stones, watch for an imagined plan taking shape before hands start, and for a structure rebuilt patiently when it tumbles.
variants.unschooling: Look for builds that solve a real problem, like a ramp for a toy car or a bed for a stuffed animal, and for a second and third version once the first one is tested.
variants.eclectic: Whether it's building bricks, cardboard or a construction kit, watch for a plan before the build, and for changes made after testing instead of starting over.

watchForNext.neutral: Comparing may turn into measuring: counting how many cups fill the jug, or how many hand spans long the table is. You might also hear them notice that a measure only works if every cup or step is the same size.

variants.charlotte_mason: In everyday life, baking, gardening or pacing out the garden bed, watch for hand spans, steps and cups used to measure, and for care taken to get the measure exactly right.
variants.classical: Watch for measuring words used precisely and in order, shortest to longest or lightest to heaviest, and for curiosity about the names of the units on the scales and ruler.
variants.montessori: After the knobbed cylinders and pink tower, watch for the child grading objects by size or weight in everyday life, and for pouring that stops right at the line.
variants.waldorf_steiner: Measurement often begins with the body here. Watch for steps, feet and hand spans used to measure a room, and for the discovery that different people's feet give different answers.
variants.unschooling: Look for measuring with a purpose in their own projects: how many scoops for the dog's dinner, whether the cubby is tall enough to stand in, or who has grown since last month.
variants.eclectic: In the kitchen or on a worksheet, watch for counting cups, spoons or steps to measure, and for interest in the numbers on the scales and the measuring jug.

watchForNext.neutral: Reactions may start to come with reasons, like 'I didn't like it when the wolf tricked them', pointing to a particular part of the story. You might also hear them wondering why a character did something, or recommending a book to someone else.

variants.charlotte_mason: In narration, listen for the child's own response to a living book coming through: a favourite character defended, or a part they want to hear again because it mattered to them.
variants.classical: After a read-aloud, listen for opinions backed by the story, 'he was brave because he went back for his friend', and for favourite passages learned by heart and recited with feeling.
variants.montessori: Watch for the child choosing books from the shelf and telling you why that one, and for them relating a character's choices to something in their own life.
variants.waldorf_steiner: After a fairy tale is told, notice which images the child carries into play, drawing or retelling, and listen for them siding with a character and saying why.
variants.unschooling: Look for reading tastes forming and being defended: a series they hunt down at the library, a character they talk about at dinner, a book they press on a sibling.
variants.eclectic: Across curriculum read-alouds and library finds, notice which ones they ask for again, and listen for the reasons: 'because the dragon was actually kind'.
